title: The Stolen Mango Grove and the Dry Leaves (ML)
summary: A dishonest landlord claims he purchased an orchard twenty years ago, presenting an aged parchment. Birbal proves the ink is fresh by examining dry leaves.
full_text:
An impoverished farmer named Kanhaiya was evicted from his family's ancestral mango orchard by a wealthy landlord, Seth Ramswaroop. The landlord presented an imperial deed of sale, written on yellowed, brittle parchment, claiming he had purchased the land from Kanhaiya's father twenty years earlier.

Kanhaiya wept before Emperor Akbar: 'Sire, my father never sold our orchard! He died five years ago, blessing me to protect our trees! The deed is a forgery!'

Akbar examined the document. The parchment looked genuinely old, stained with yellow age spots and frayed at the edges.

Akbar handed the parchment to Birbal. Birbal inspected the document with a jeweler's magnifying lens, smelled the parchment, and held it up to the sunlight.

Birbal asked the landlord: 'Seth Ramswaroop, when was this deed written?'

'Exactly twenty years ago, my lord, in the presence of the village council.'

Birbal smiled calmly: 'Your Majesty, the parchment itself is indeed old—perhaps thirty years old, salvaged from an old ledger. But the black ink written upon it is less than two weeks old!'

The landlord protested: 'How can you claim that? Ink is ink!'

Birbal ordered a bowl of warm water and a fresh white blotting cloth. He gently pressed the damp cloth against one of the ink letters on the deed.

The ink immediately bled, transferring a sharp purple stain onto the white cloth!

Birbal explained:

'Ancient Indian ink prepared twenty years ago was made of soot, iron gall, and acacia gum. Once dried for over five years, it oxidizes and hardens into the fiber of the parchment, becoming completely water-resistant!

'Only fresh synthetic ink, mixed with aniline dyes introduced to the market last month, dissolves and stains a damp cloth! This deed was written two weeks ago on antique paper to forge an ancient date!'

The landlord fell to the floor in terror, confessing that he had hired a forger in the bazaar to steal the poor farmer's orchard.

Akbar ordered the landlord heavily fined, imprisoned for five years, and returned the land to the rightful farmer, praising Birbal's forensic brilliance.
